virtue: For worthless things they exchange what is valuable
rubric_v1_gloss: “For worthless things they exchange what is valuable.”
source_scope: Swapping one's own poor goods for someone else's good ones, in trade or by stealth. The Qing teaching commentaries read 惡 and 好 as bad and good things.

teaching.context: Among the tract's evil-doers (以惡易好):
teaching.quote: They endanger others to save themselves. … They impoverish others for their own gain. … For worthless things they exchange what is valuable.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. Suzuki and Carus (1906), characters 503–514

teaching.quote: 惡，是不好的物。凡遇貨物，把自己不堪的，暗裡頭換了人好的，奸巧同上。○對面看來，善人看破外物無常，美惡不消計較，如薛包與眾弟分財，田屋只取荒破的，奴僕只取老衰的，器物只取壞敗的
teaching.citation: 太上感應篇直講 (Qing vernacular lectures; Wikisource text)

teaching.explanation: Project translation: 'Bad means things that are no good. Whenever goods are involved, secretly swapping one's own useless things for another person's good ones is the same crafty trickery as above. Seen from the other side, the good person sees through the impermanence of outward things and does not haggle over fine and poor: like Xue Bao, who in dividing property with his brothers took only the waste fields and broken houses, the old and feeble servants and the damaged utensils.'

teaching.quote: 物有美惡，人情愛憎因之。若以低醜之物，換人好物，是卽穿窬之行也。宋蘇軾珍藏一美玉，章持求觀，因以燕石換去。
teaching.citation: 太上感應篇集註 (Qing collected notes; Wikisource text)

teaching.explanation: Project translation: 'Things are fine or poor, and people's likes and dislikes follow them. To exchange a low, ugly thing for someone else's good thing is the conduct of a burglar. Su Shi of the Song treasured a fine jade; Zhang Chi asked to see it and swapped it for a worthless Yan stone.'

teaching.context: Balfour's 1884 translation renders the same four characters differently:
teaching.quote: returns evil for good
teaching.citation: Balfour, Taoist Texts (1884), Book of Recompenses, p. 105

teaching.explanation: Balfour's reading concerns repaying kindness with harm, not an exchange of goods. The two Qing teaching commentaries both take 以惡易好 as swapping bad goods for good, the reading followed here. The vice is a covert, one-sided exchange; its contrary is taking the worse share oneself.

limits: The tract gives only four characters. This guide follows Suzuki and Carus and the commentaries; Balfour's 'returns evil for good' is a different translation. Fair exchange openly agreed, or a bad bargain made knowingly, is not this vice.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
gave away whatsoever is in the world considered most difficult to bestow

Full passage:
He [king Vessantara] had given up, O king, the caring for himself, and devoted himself thenceforth to caring for others alone. His mind was fixed immovably on the thought: “How can I make all beings to be at peace, healthy, and wealthy, and long lived ?” ... he [king Vessantara] gave not for the sake of rebirth in any glorious state, he gave not for the sake of wealth, nor of receiving gifts in return, nor of flattery, nor of long life for himself, nor of high birth, nor of happiness, nor of power, nor of fame, nor of offspring either of daughters or of sons—but it was for the sake of supreme wisdom and of the treasure thereof that he gave gifts so immense, so immeasurable, so unsurpassed. It was when he had attained to that supreme wisdom that he uttered the verse :

“Gâli, my son, and the Black Antelope,

My daughter, and my queen, my wife, Maddi,

I gave them all away without a thought—

And ’twas for Buddhahood I did this thing.’”

... king Vessantara gave away whatsoever is in the world considered most difficult to bestow ... And there was never another giving, O king, which had such power as that generosity of the great king Vessantara. ... And it was on the giving of [king Vessantara’s gift], O king, that the broad earth shook seven times.
examples.reason: Gave vast gifts and recalls them without regret; directly fits the injunction.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct shows this virtue.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
kneels at the feet of the Saint, and implores that the Saint will pour out prayer for him to the Lord. Then, being first reproved by him (the Saint) for certain sins of his, he exercised repentance, and promised to amend thenceforth.

Full passage:
In the same period Conall, bishop in Coleraine, collected wellnigh countless presents from the people of the plain of Eilne (between the rivers Bush and Bann), and prepared a hospitable reception for the blessed man [Columba] on his return after the conference of the above-mentioned kings, with a great multitude following him. Then the many presents of the people, laid in the courtyard of the monastery, are given to the holy man to be blessed on his arrival. And while he is looking upon them as he blesses them, he specially points out the present of a certain rich man, and ... says, ‘The mercy of God attendeth the man whose present this is, for his charities to the poor, and for his liberality.’ ... But that liberal rich man of the name of Brendan, of whose present we have spoken a little above, himself also hearing the words of the Saint spoken concerning him, kneels at the feet of the Saint, and implores that the Saint will pour out prayer for him to the Lord. Then, being first reproved by him (the Saint) for certain sins of his, he exercised repentance, and promised to amend thenceforth. And so each one was amended and cured of his own special vices.
examples.reason: No gift is made or regretted in the selected act.
examples.evidence_level: Neither direction is established by the described conduct.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
gives a benefit to just anybody

Full passage:
If someone [an indiscriminate giver] gives a benefit to just anybody, then it is appreciated by no one. No one thinks of himself as the personal guest of the innkeeper or tavern keeper, nor the companion of the man who gives a public feast. In those cases one [a recipient] can legitimately say, "Well, what has he given to me? Just this, I guess: exactly what he also gave to the person he hardly knows and even to his enemies and the most dishonorable of people. Surely you do not think he judged me worthy of anything, do you? He was only indulging his vice." If you want something to be appreciated, make it rare. No one minds being in debt on those terms. But no one should think that I [Seneca] am reducing generosity and keeping it on a tight leash. Let generosity go as far as it likes-but it should go and not just wander around. One may spread it around, but only in such a way that each and every recipient feels that he is not just one of the crowd, even if he has received the gift along with many others. ... In fact I do not impose obstacles to the giving of benefits. The more and the greater they are, the more praise they bring to the giver. But let there be some exercise of good judgment. After all, things given haphazardly and recklessly will not endear themselves to anyone.
examples.reason: He gives freely; no regret shown. Line says nothing about discrimination.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct shows this virtue.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
A certain wealthy man designed to annoy the ascetic. So he brought him to his dwelling, and pointed out a seat, and then served him with fish. After the meal, the man sat on one side, and said, "This food was prepared on purpose for you, by killing living creatures. Not upon my head is this wrong, but upon yours!"

Full passage:
Once on a time, when Brahmadatta was king of Benares, the Bodhisatta was born a brahmin. When he came of age he embraced the religious life.

He came down from Himalaya to get salt and seasoning, and next day walked the city, begging alms. A certain wealthy man designed to annoy the ascetic. So he brought him to his

dwelling, and pointed out a seat, and then served him with fish. After the meal, the man sat on one side, and said,

"This food was prepared on purpose for you, by killing living creatures. Not upon my head is this wrong, but upon yours!" And he repeated the first stanza:--

"The wicked kills, and cooks, and gives to eat:

He is defiled with sin that takes such meat." On hearing this, the Bodhisatta recited the second stanza:--

"The wicked may for gift slay wife or son,

Yet, if the holy eat, no sin is done."

...

And the Bodhisatta with these words of instruction rose from his seat and departed.
examples.reason: He gives but immediately turns gift into accusation; not regret exactly, but begrudging spirit evident.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct conflicts with this virtue.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
He opened the hand of liberality, displayed his munificence, and bestowed innumerable gifts upon his troops and people.

Full passage:
A prince inherited immense riches by succeeding to his father. He opened the hand of liberality, displayed his munificence, and bestowed innumerable gifts upon his troops and people. "The brain will not be perfumed by a censer of green aloes-wood; place it over the fire that it may diffuse fragrance like ambergris. If ambitious of a great name, make a practice of munificence, for the crop will not shoot till thou shalt sow the seed."

A narrow-minded courtier began to admonish him, saying, "Verily, former sovereigns have collected this wealth with scrupulosity and stored it advisedly. Check your hand in this waste, for accidents wait ahead, and foes lurk behind. God forbid that you should want it on a day of need.--Wert thou to distribute the contents of a granary among the people, every master of a family might receive a grain of rice; why not exact a grain of silver from each, that thou mightest daily hoard a chamber full of treasure?"

The prince turned his face aside from this speech, so contrary to his own lofty sentiments, and harshly reprimanded him, saying, "A great and glorious God made me sovereign of this property, that I might enjoy and spend it; and posted me not a sentinel, to hoard and watch over it.--Carown perished, who possessed forty magazines of treasure; Nushirowan died not, who left behind him a fair reputation."
examples.reason: He gives abundantly and firmly refuses to regret it when admonished, matching the injunction well.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct shows this virtue.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest. ... And he would not: but went and cast him into prison, till he should pay the debt.

Full passage:
Then came Peter to him, and said, Lord, how oft shall my brother sin against me, and I forgive him? till seven times? Jesus saith unto him, I say not unto thee, Until seven times: but, Until seventy times seven.

Therefore is the kingdom of heaven likened unto a certain king, which would take account of his servants.

And when he had begun to reckon, one [a servant] was brought unto him, which owed him ten thousand talents.

But forasmuch as he had not to pay, his lord commanded him to be sold, and his wife, and children, and all that he had, and payment to be made.

The servant therefore fell down, and worshipped him, saying, Lord, have patience with me, and I will pay thee all.

Then the lord of that servant was moved with compassion, and loosed him, and forgave him the debt.

But the same servant went out, and found one of his fellowservants, which owed him an hundred pence: and he laid hands on him, and took him by the throat, saying, Pay me that thou owest.

And his fellowservant fell down at his feet, and besought him, saying, Have patience with me, and I will pay thee all.

And he would not: but went and cast him into prison, till he should pay the debt.

So when his fellowservants saw what was done, they were very sorry, and came and told unto their lord all that was done.

Then his lord [the king], after that he had called him, said unto him, O thou wicked servant, I forgave thee all that debt, because thou desiredst me: Shouldest not thou also have had compassion on thy fellowservant, even as I had pity on thee? And his lord was wroth, and delivered him to the tormentors, till he should pay all that was due unto him.

So likewise shall my heavenly Father do also unto you, if ye from your hearts forgive not every one his brother their trespasses.
examples.reason: He neither gives nor shows any ungrudging spirit; he grudges a trivial sum. The line mainly concerns regretting gifts already made, so this is some conflict rather than the clearest case.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct conflicts with this virtue.

source_scope: Getting rich by improper means and then being arrogant with it. The Chinese 驕 means arrogance; Suzuki and Carus render it 'remain vulgar', Balfour 'arrogant'.

teaching.context: Among the tract's evil-doers (苟富而驕):
teaching.quote: Improperly they have grown rich, and withal they remain vulgar.

teaching.context: Balfour's translation of the same entry:
teaching.quote: if he is arrogant on the score of ill-gotten gains
teaching.citation: Balfour, Taoist Texts (1884), Book of Recompenses, p. 105

teaching.quote: 非義而致富，謂之苟富。如剝人肥己，僥倖獲財，皆是也。大抵冒越之利，鬼神所忌，因福致禍，往往有之，况可以之驕人耶？
teaching.citation: 太上感應篇集註 (Qing collected notes; Wikisource text)

teaching.explanation: Project translation: 'Getting rich without righteousness is called improper riches: fleecing others to fatten oneself, or getting wealth by a lucky chance. Profit that oversteps is what ghosts and spirits abhor, and it often turns good fortune into disaster; how much worse to use it to be arrogant toward others?'

teaching.quote: 苟富，是苟且致富，如盤剝小民，僥倖得財，都是過分的財，鬼神最忌，況且無一善狀，那能免禍。○對面看來，善人如范文正公，掘了藏，分毫不取，後來得俸銀數萬，買田千畝做義田，存活貧族
teaching.citation: 太上感應篇直講 (Qing vernacular lectures; Wikisource text)

teaching.explanation: Project translation: 'Improper riches means getting rich by expedient means, such as squeezing the common people with interest or getting wealth by luck: all wealth beyond one's due, which spirits most abhor; and if there is not a single good deed besides, how can disaster be avoided? Seen from the other side, the good person is like Fan Zhongyan: when he dug up buried treasure he took not a hair of it, and later, receiving salary silver in the tens of thousands, he bought a thousand mu as charitable fields to keep his poor kin alive.'

teaching.quote: Those who seize property, are, to use an illustration, like those who relieve their hunger by eating tainted meat, or quench their thirst by drinking poisoned liquor.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. Suzuki and Carus (1906), characters 1146–1169

teaching.explanation: The entry joins two faults: wealth gained improperly, by exploitation or an undeserved windfall the commentaries call beyond one's due, and the arrogance built on it. Their good example is not poverty but righteous use: refusing treasure that is not one's own and spending wealth on poor kin.

limits: Suzuki and Carus's 'remain vulgar' obscures 驕 (arrogance); this guide follows the Chinese and the commentaries. Honest wealth is not condemned, and arrogance alone falls under other entries. The commentaries count even a lucky windfall as improper; that is their reading.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
Because of that, the first monk became resentful. Soon afterwards the other monk was very thirsty. He asked the resentful monk to borrow his water filter. He refused and the other monk died from thirst.

Full passage:
On one occasion, there were two monks traveling through the Kosalan country.

One monk [the resentful monk] misbehaved,

and the other monk said to him,

“Don’t do that.

It’s not allowable.”

Because of that, the first monk became resentful.

Soon afterwards the other monk was very thirsty. He asked the resentful monk

to borrow his water filter.

He refused

and the other monk died from thirst.

When the resentful monk arrived at the monastery, he told the monks what had happened.

“So you refused to lend your water filter when asked?”

“Yes.”

The monks of few desires complained and criticized him,

“How could a monk do such a thing?”

They told the Buddha.

Soon afterwards the Buddha had the monks gathered and questioned that monk:

“Is it true, monk, that you did this?”

“It’s true, sir.”

The Buddha rebuked him,

“It’s not suitable, foolish man, it’s not proper, it’s not worthy of a monastic, it’s not allowable, it’s not to be done.

How could you refuse to lend your water filter when asked?

This will affect people’s confidence …”

After rebuking him …

the Buddha gave a teaching and addressed the monks:

“If you’re traveling with a monk and he asks to borrow your water filter, you should lend it.

If you don’t, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.

On the other hand, you shouldn’t travel without a water filter.

If you do, you commit an offense of wrong conduct.

If there’s no water filter or strainer, you should determine a corner of your robe:

‘I’ll drink after filtering with this.’”
examples.reason: Took offence at rebuke and held a grudge acted on lethally; clear conflict.
examples.evidence_level: Clear evidence that the conduct conflicts with this virtue.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
he received no answer at all. ... willingly, even joyfully, Macarius used to speak to such a man of whatever he wished to hear.

Full passage:
When anyone came respectfully to the abbot Macarius, desiring to hear some exhortation from ... him [the abbot Macarius], he received no answer at all. But if anyone came despising Macarius and did violence to him with such words as these, "Lo you there, father Macarius! You used to be a camel-driver, and steal the natron. How your master used to beat you when he caught you robbing him!" willingly, even joyfully, Macarius used to speak to such a man of whatever he wished to hear.
examples.reason: Both parts are met: he endures the humiliation, and he bears no grudge, since he helps the insulter gladly.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct shows this virtue.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
whilst unfolding in cunning words his pretended embassy, he started up on a sudden, and unsheathing the dagger under his garment, assaulted the king.

Full passage:
The next year there came into the province one called Eumer, sent by the king of the West-Saxons, whose name was Cuichelm, to lie in wait for King Edwin, in hopes at once to deprive him of his kingdom and his life. He had a two-edged dagger, dipped in poison, to the end that, if the wound inflicted by the weapon did not avail to kill the king, it might be aided by the deadly venom. He came to the king on the first day of the Easter festival, at the river Derwent, where there was then a royal township, and being admitted as if to deliver a message from his master, whilst unfolding in cunning words his pretended embassy, he started up on a sudden, and unsheathing the dagger under his garment, assaulted the king. When Lilla, the king’s most devoted servant, saw this, having no buckler at hand to protect the king from death, he at once interposed his own body to receive the blow; but the enemy struck home with such force, that he wounded the king through the body of the slaughtered thegn. Being then attacked on all sides with swords, in the confusion he also slew impiously with his dagger another of the thegns, whose name was Forthhere.
examples.reason: The passage shows no humiliation suffered by Eumer. The assassination is hostile, but whether he holds a grudge is not stated.
examples.evidence_level: Neither direction is established by the described conduct.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
They prevailed upon Thondarie, a woman entirely devoted to their interests, to spread the rumour that she had spent a night in the apartments of Buddha.

Full passage:
While the most excellent Buddha was in the Dzetawon monastery, the heretics of Thawattie made another attempt to lower, nay, to destroy his reputation. They prevailed upon Thondarie, a woman entirely devoted to their interests, to spread the rumour that she had spent a night in the apartments of Buddha. When the calumny had been noised abroad, they suborned a gang of drunkards, to whom they promised a large sum of money, if they would do away with the instrument of the slander. They accordingly selected a favourable opportunity, killed Thondarie, and threw her body into a cluster of bushes close to the monastery. When the crime had been perpetrated, the heretics raised a cry all over the country inquiring about Thondarie. She could nowhere be found. Search was made in every direction, until at last, by the secret directions of their emissaries, the body was found on the spot where it had been apparently concealed. The party hostile to Buddha laid the crime at his door. The king of the country, urged on by them, ordered a strict inquiry to be made. ... Heated by the liquor they [the perpetrators of the deed] had taken, they began to accuse each other of having killed Thondarie. Their conversation was overheard by one of the king's servants, who had them arrested and led to the palace. ... Indignant at such a horrible deed, the king ordered the murderers and their advisers to be put to death. ... Buddha told his disciples that what had happened on this melancholy occasion was but a just retribution for his having in a former existence been drunk, and in that state abused and slandered a holy personage.
examples.reason: Their repeated attempt to destroy the Buddha's reputation suggests grudge-bearing rivalry, though no humiliation of them is stated.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct conflicts with this virtue.

examples.agent: one of them which were with Jesus
examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest’s, and smote off his ear

Full passage:
And while he [Jesus] yet spake, lo, Judas, one of the twelve, came, and with him a great multitude with swords and staves, from the chief priests and elders of the people. ... Now he [Judas] that betrayed him gave them a sign, saying, Whomsoever I shall kiss, that same is he: hold him fast. ... Then came they [the multitude], and laid hands on Jesus and took him. ... And, behold, one of them which were with Jesus stretched out his hand, and drew his sword, and struck a servant of the high priest’s, and smote off his ear. ... Then said Jesus unto him, Put up again thy sword into his place: for all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword. ... Thinkest thou that I cannot now pray to my Father, and he shall presently give me more than twelve legions of angels? ... But how then shall the scriptures be fulfilled, that thus it must be? ... In that same hour said Jesus to the multitudes, Are ye come out as against a thief with swords and staves for to take me? I sat daily with you teaching in the temple, and ye laid no hold on me. ... But all this was done, that the scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled.
examples.reason: Retaliating with violence rather than enduring fails the 'endurance' part. The humiliation was mainly his master's, and no lasting grudge is shown.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct conflicts with this virtue.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
Still personating the thief, he took his parents into the thick forest, threw them down, and left them there, after which he returned to his wife.

Full passage:
In a former age, Mugalan was called Sumana, at which time his parents were blind ; but he was very attentive to them, and devoted to them all his time. ... After he [Sumana] brought his wife home, ... She [Sumana's wife] soon became discontented ; to deceive Sumana she put filth upon the hair of his parents, and said they had done it themselves after they were combed. As she insisted upon being allowed to return to her village, her husband was overcome, and he resolved upon putting his parents out of the way. To effect this, he took them to a certain forest, under the pretence of letting them visit some of their friends ; and when they had arrived at a lonely place, he gave the reins of the animals by which they were drawn into the hands of his parents, and said that he must go forward a little to see if there were any robbers near the road, as it was a dangerous spot. He then imitated the onset of a robber, and his parents, thinking that some one else was attacking them, called out to him not to think about them, but to make his own escape. Still personating the thief, he took his parents into the thick forest, threw them down, and left them there, after which he returned to his wife. For this crime he was born continually in hell, during hundreds of thousands of years ; but on his release therefrom, on account of his previous merit, and ... because he [Sumana] was free from any other crime, in the time of Gotama he became one of the two principal disciples of Budha.
examples.reason: He was deceived but no humiliation endurance is tested; he does not endure the household strain and acts destructively. Grudge against parents not stated.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct conflicts with this virtue.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
Accordingly, he climbed over walls and broke into houses, grabbing everything he could see or lay hands upon.

Full passage:
Mr. Kuo of the Ch'i State was very rich, while Mr. Hsiang of the Sung State was very poor. The latter travelled from Sung to Ch'i and asked the other for the secret of his prosperity. Mr. Kuo told him. "It is because I am a good thief," he said. ... Mr. Hsiang was overjoyed; he understood the word "thief" in its literal sense, but he did not understand the true way of becoming a thief. Accordingly, he climbed over walls and broke into houses, grabbing everything he could see or lay hands upon. But before very long his thefts brought him into trouble, and he was stripped even of what he had previously possessed. Thinking that Mr. Kuo had basely deceived him, Hsiang went to him with a bitter complaint. ... Well, the things that I [Mr. Kuo] steal are the riches of Heaven and earth, each in their season ... Mr. Hsiang, ... went off to consult Tung Kuo, a man of learning. Tung Kuo said to him: "... Mr. Kuo's thefts are carried out in a spirit of justice, and therefore bring no retribution. But your thefts were carried out in a spirit of self-seeking and therefore landed you in trouble. Those who take possession of property, whether public or private, are thieves. ... [People] who abstain from taking property, public or private, are also thieves. ... The great principle of Heaven and earth is to treat public property as such and private property as such. ..."
examples.reason: Literally broke into houses taking everything, exactly the injunction.
examples.evidence_level: Clear evidence that the conduct shows this vice.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
her husband was overcome, and he resolved upon putting his parents out of the way. ... Still personating the thief, he took his parents into the thick forest, threw them down, and left them there, after which he returned to his wife.

Full passage:
In a former age, Mugalan was called Sumana, at which time his parents were blind ; but he was very attentive to them, and devoted to them all his time. ... After he [Sumana] brought his wife home, ... She [Sumana's wife] soon became discontented ; to deceive Sumana she put filth upon the hair of his parents, and said they had done it themselves after they were combed. As she insisted upon being allowed to return to her village, her husband was overcome, and he resolved upon putting his parents out of the way. To effect this, he took them to a certain forest, under the pretence of letting them visit some of their friends ; and when they had arrived at a lonely place, he gave the reins of the animals by which they were drawn into the hands of his parents, and said that he must go forward a little to see if there were any robbers near the road, as it was a dangerous spot. He then imitated the onset of a robber, and his parents, thinking that some one else was attacking them, called out to him not to think about them, but to make his own escape. Still personating the thief, he took his parents into the thick forest, threw them down, and left them there, after which he returned to his wife. For this crime he was born continually in hell, during hundreds of thousands of years ; but on his release therefrom, on account of his previous merit, and ... because he [Sumana] was free from any other crime, in the time of Gotama he became one of the two principal disciples of Budha.
examples.reason: There is no house-breaking or seizure of valuables.
examples.evidence_level: Neither direction is established by the described conduct.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
sat down and forged more than fifty “licentious letters” intended to slander the reputation of the founder of that rival school. ... Diotimus portrayed Epicurus as some kind of depraved maniac ... in order to bolster his arguments against the philosophy. ... Diotimus chose to respond to slander with slander. He decided to commit a crime worse than what Apollodorus was falsely alleging against Chrysippus.

Full passage:
Sometime around the turn of the first century BC, as the philosophies of Epicurus enjoyed a resurgence in Athens ... Diotimus [the Stoic philosopher] sat down and forged more than fifty “licentious letters” intended to slander the reputation of the founder of that rival school. ... Diotimus portrayed Epicurus as some kind of depraved maniac ... in order to bolster his arguments against the philosophy.

Part of the motivation was no doubt self-defense. The Epicurean school at this time was ascendant, and under the leadership of the prolific Apollodorus, who ... was nicknamed “the Garden Tyrant.” We are told by Diogenes Laërtius that Apollodorus had taken to smearing Chrysippus, claiming that the Stoic had filled his books with quotes he had stolen from others. Such slander of the Stoa’s great fighter would need to be addressed.

Diotimus chose to respond to slander with slander. He decided to commit a crime worse than what Apollodorus was falsely alleging against Chrysippus.

For a school that prized logic and truth as much as virtuous behavior, Diotimus’s actions would have been inexcusable. Even if Epicureanism was now posing some kind of existential threat to Stoicism, it hardly justifies the commission of literary fraud. ...

Athenaeus, citing Demetrius of Magnesia, says that Zeno of Sidon, who succeeded Apollodorus as head of the Epicurean school, tracked Diotimus down and filed suit against him. The court sided with Zeno of Sidon and sentenced Diotimus to death, which is a rather extreme form of justice—and certainly not one Rome would have countenanced.

While it’s unlikely that the death penalty would have been given for something as common as slander, there can be no doubt that a strong fine and exile from Athens were imposed. And greater than that, a personal shame.
examples.reason: There is no house-breaking or theft.
examples.evidence_level: Neither direction is established by the described conduct.

Stephen Dubner and Steven Levitt published the work of an anonymous economist turned bagelseller , Paul F., who dropped off baskets of bagels and came back to collect money from a cashbox, and also collected statistics on payment rates.  The current average payment rate is 89%.  Paul F. found that people on the executive floor of a company steal more bagels; that people with security clearances don't steal any fewer bagels; that telecom companies have robbed him and that law firms aren't worth the trouble. ... Others value their integrity less than a bagel.

examples.story:
Selected act or disposition (quoted from the passage):
Dauna abstracted one of the canine teeth and concealed it in the folds of his turban.

Full passage:
They [the Malla princes] agreed that, the relics of Buddha being the most valuable possessions in the world, they would not part with them. Many angry words were exchanged among contending parties. They were almost ready to draw the sword when a celebrated pounha, named Dauna, made his appearance. He stood on an elevated spot, and making a sign with his hand, began to speak in a language calculated to soothe the irritation of the parties. ... I will divide the relics into eight equal portions. ... Dauna went on explaining more fully ... The kings [the contending parties], on hearing the words of Dauna, came to the ... place where he stood, and entreated him to make eight equal portions of the relics. Dauna assented to their request. They went with him to the place of the relics. ... They [the princes] all wept and lamented. Whilst they were overwhelmed with grief, Dauna abstracted one of the canine teeth and concealed it in the folds of his turban. All the relics were duly apportioned to all the kings. A Thagia, who had seen the doing of Dauna, took adroitly the tooth, and without being perceived carried it into the Nats' seats, and placed it in the Dzoolamani dzedi. When the partition was over, Dauna was surprised not to find the tooth he had stolen: he did not, however, dare to complain, as his pious fraud would have been discovered. To console himself for such a loss, he asked for the possession of the golden vessel wherein the relics had been kept. His demand was favourably received, and the golden vessel was given to him.
examples.reason: He stole but did not break into houses; the specific vice is not shown, though property-taking is adjacent.
examples.evidence_level: Some evidence that the conduct shows this vice.

Full passage:
And Jesus entered and passed through Jericho. ... And, behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus, which was the chief among the publicans, and he was rich. ... And he sought to see Jesus who he was; and could not for the press, because he was little of stature. ... And he ran before, and climbed up into a sycomore tree to see him: for he was to pass that way. ... And when Jesus came to the place, he looked up, and saw him, and said unto him, Zacchaeus, make haste, and come down; for to day I must abide at thy house. ... And he made haste, and came down, and received him joyfully. ... And when they saw it, they all murmured, saying, That he was gone to be guest with a man that is a sinner. ... And Zacchaeus stood, and said unto the Lord: Behold, Lord, the half of my goods I give to the poor; and if I have taken any thing from any man by false accusation, I restore him fourfold. ... And Jesus said unto him, This day is salvation come to this house, forsomuch as he also is a son of Abraham. ... For the Son of man is come to seek and to save that which was lost.
examples.reason: Housebreaking is not involved. Returning wrongly taken property only loosely opposes the seizure of others' valuables, so the evidence is mostly neither, with a slight lean toward resistance.

id: taoist|ganying_pian|They do many clandestine and wrong deeds
list_name: Treatise on Action and Response: the moral injunctions and every numbered evil deed (Suzuki and Carus)
virtue: They do many clandestine and wrong deeds
rubric_v1_gloss: “They do many clandestine and wrong deeds.”
source_scope: Deeds that are both clandestine and wrong (行多隱僻). Suzuki and Carus: 'clandestine and wrong'; Balfour: 'occult or secret practices'; the Qing teaching commentaries: conduct that is not open and not upright.

teaching.quote: They do many clandestine and wrong deeds.

teaching.quote: if he is addicted to occult or secret practices
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. Frederic H. Balfour(1884), p 106

teaching.quote: it is apparent that heaven and earth are possessed of crime-recording spirits.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. D. T. Suzuki and Paul Carus (1906)

teaching.context: The Qing Plain Lectures on the tract:
teaching.quote: 隱，是不光明。僻，是不正大。瞞心昧己，只向暗僻中，做貪利邪淫，損人等事，這句最是暗空虧心的惡。○對面看來，善人生平做事，件件可對人說的，就是積陰德，也不是故意揀人不見聞的事做。
teaching.citation: 太上感應篇直講 (Qing vernacular lectures; Wikisource text)

teaching.explanation: Project translation: '隱 means not open to the light; 僻 means not upright. Deceiving their own hearts, they do greedy, lewd and harmful things only in dark, out-of-the-way places; this is the most hidden and conscience-betraying evil. Seen from the other side, the good person does things each of which could be told to others; even in storing up hidden merit, they do not deliberately pick what others will not see or hear.'

teaching.quote: 隱僻非止一事，如姦盜邪淫之類，凡不可使天知，不可對人言者，皆是也。
teaching.citation: 太上感應篇集註 (Qing collected notes; Wikisource text)

teaching.explanation: Project translation: 'Hidden and crooked deeds are not one thing only: adultery, theft, lewdness and the like. Whatever cannot be let known to heaven or told to others is all of it.'

The vice joins secrecy to wrong. The commentaries' test, whether a deed could be told to others, is applied to wrongful deeds such as theft and lewdness; the Plain Lectures count good done without seeking recognition as open and upright, not hidden. Balfour's 'occult or secret practices' sits among his list of taboo observances and is a different reading, kept separate.

limits: Secrecy by itself is not wrongdoing, and the Plain Lectures do not count good done without seeking recognition as hidden. Not doing a hidden wrong counts as resistance in these examples only when the scene supplies the chance and the choice. Balfour's 'occult' is a translation variant. The English of the Qing commentaries is project translation.

id: taoist|ganying_pian|With heresies they mislead others
list_name: Treatise on Action and Response: the moral injunctions and every numbered evil deed (Suzuki and Carus)
virtue: With heresies they mislead others
rubric_v1_gloss: “With heresies they mislead others.”
source_scope: Using 'left ways' (左道), sorcery and pretended revelation, to delude people, usually for money or a following. The Qing commentaries define it by deception, not by belonging to a different one of the three teachings.

teaching.context: Among the tract's evil-doers (左道惑眾):
teaching.quote: With heresies they mislead others.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. Suzuki and Carus (1906), characters 875–878

teaching.context: Balfour's translation of the same entry:
teaching.quote: puts them in positions of perplexity by left-handed dealings
teaching.citation: Balfour, Taoist Texts (1884), Book of Recompenses, p. 106

teaching.quote: 不正之道，謂之左道。三教聖人，道雖不同，上者使人明心見性，其次使人遷善遠惡，未有好爲詭異以惑人者。凡惑人者，皆左道也。葢人心多愚，最易惑以禍福。一爲所惑，因而生盜、生姦，甚則聚黨作亂。
teaching.citation: 太上感應篇集註 (Qing collected notes; Wikisource text)

teaching.explanation: Project translation: 'A way that is not upright is called a left way. The sages of the three teachings differ in their ways, but the highest make people understand their minds and see their natures, and the next make people turn to good and away from evil; none of them loves the uncanny so as to delude people. All who delude people are left ways. People's minds are often foolish and most easily deluded with threats of calamity and promises of fortune. Once deluded, theft and adultery arise from it, and at worst they gather factions and rise in revolt.' Its example: schemers coached a simple villager to proclaim himself a god come down and gathered crowds' offerings to avert calamity, until the prefect broke it up.

teaching.quote: 左道是妖術，小如歸香歸教等類，大如白蓮教之類，都是奸民燒香說法，搖惑愚民；小則淫汙，大則倡亂國法，或用刑除，或用兵滅。
teaching.citation: 太上感應篇直講 (Qing vernacular lectures; Wikisource text)

teaching.explanation: Project translation: 'Left ways are sorcery: small ones like the incense-joining sects, great ones like the White Lotus teaching. All are wicked people burning incense and preaching to sway the ignorant; at the small end, lewdness; at the great end, rebellion against the law of the state, to be removed by punishment or wiped out by troops.' Its contrary, in the same lecture, is spreading the upright teaching openly, by founding schools for poor students and printing good books to give away.

The fault lies in deluding people, with sorcery, false revelations or threats of calamity, to get money, followers or licence. The commentaries explicitly exempt the differing ways of the three teachings; open, honest teaching is the remedy.

limits: 'Heresy' is Suzuki and Carus's word; in the commentaries 左道 means sorcery and deceptive cults. The Plain Lectures endorse suppressing the White Lotus and similar sects by punishment or troops; that is its historical position, recorded here, not a standard for judging peaceful religious difference. Sincere teaching of another religion is not shown to be this vice by these sources.

teaching.quote: With the members of their own family they are angry and quarrelsome.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. D. T. Suzuki and Paul Carus(1906)

teaching.quote: or wrangles and quarrels with his own flesh and blood
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. Frederic H. Balfour(1884), pp 105–106

teaching.quote: The term “bone and flesh” in Chinese means “family relations.”
teaching.citation: Suzuki/Carus,1944 printing, explanatory notes p.76

limits: Own kin is the target; an unrelated dispute is not this vice.

id: taoist|ganying_pian|With unrestrained barbarism they kill and stab
list_name: Treatise on Action and Response: the moral injunctions and every numbered evil deed (Suzuki and Carus)
virtue: With unrestrained barbarism they kill and stab
rubric_v1_gloss: “With unrestrained barbarism they kill and stab.”
source_scope: Unrestrained violent killing and wounding (Suzuki). Balfour has compliance with tyrannical designs.

teaching.quote: With unrestrained barbarism they kill and … stab.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. D. T. Suzuki and Paul Carus (1906)

teaching.quote: … and complies with tyrannical designs to kill or wound …
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. Frederic H. Balfour (1884), p 105

limits: The supplied text does not address self-defense or lawful force. The qualifiers 'unrestrained' and 'tyrannical' matter.

id: taoist|ganying_pian|With violence they seize, with violence they demand
list_name: Treatise on Action and Response: the moral injunctions and every numbered evil deed (Suzuki and Carus)
virtue: With violence they seize, with violence they demand
rubric_v1_gloss: “With violence they seize, with violence they demand.”
source_scope: Seizing things or demanding them by force.

teaching.quote: With violence they seize, with violence they demand.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. D. T. Suzuki and Paul Carus(1906)

teaching.quote: …takes away other people's property by main force, or insists upon it being given up-bent on getting it by hook or by crook…
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. Frederic H. Balfour(1884), pp 105–106

limits: The means is violence. Lawful, non-violent requests are not this vice.

id: taoist|ganying_pian|Without festive occasions they prepare cattle for food
list_name: Treatise on Action and Response: the moral injunctions and every numbered evil deed (Suzuki and Carus)
virtue: Without festive occasions they prepare cattle for food
rubric_v1_gloss: “Without festive occasions they prepare cattle for food.”
source_scope: Slaughtering without festive occasion (Suzuki). Balfour has 'without regard to the proprieties'.

teaching.quote: Without festive occasions they prepare … cattle for food.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. D. T. Suzuki and Paul Carus (1906)

teaching.quote: … slaughters animals without regard to the proprieties …
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. Frederic H. Balfour (1884), p 105

teaching.quote: It is customary in China to kill cattle on festivals only, and it is considered improper … to slay cattle for food without due occasion.
teaching.citation: Suzuki/Carus,1944 printing, explanatory notes p.76

limits: Note 41 (1944 witness) attributes the rule to a custom of the translators' time: festivals or due occasion. It is not a vegetarian rule or a current universal ethnographic fact. The two translations' qualifiers differ.

list_name: Treatise on Action and Response: the moral injunctions and every numbered evil deed (Suzuki and Carus)
virtue: Yet there are some people whose behavior is unrighteous
rubric_v1_gloss: “Yet there are some people whose behavior is unrighteous.”
source_scope: Vice item opening the tract's description of evil-doers: unrighteous behavior in general.

teaching.quote: Yet there are some people whose behavior is unrighteous.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. D. T. Suzuki and Paul Carus (1906)

teaching.quote: Their deportment is irrational. … In evil they delight. … With brutality they do harm and damage.
teaching.citation: Ganying Pian, trans. D. T. Suzuki and Paul Carus (1906)

limits: 'Unrighteous' is not defined beyond the listed deeds. High scores mean resistance. Absence of a vice is not resistance.
